note: long English narrative passage
text:
The lighthouse at Cape Marrow had not been lit in eleven years, and yet every evening, as the fog came rolling in from the grey sea, the villagers swore they could see a faint amber glow behind the cracked glass of the lantern room. Old Tomasz, who had kept the light until his knees gave out, would sit on the bench outside the bakery and shake his head. "It is the reflection of the sunset," he would say, "nothing more." But the children knew better, and so did the fishermen, who steered their small boats by that glow when the weather turned and the rocks hid beneath the waves.

On the first night of November, a stranger arrived on the last bus from the city. She carried a single leather satchel and a folded map that she did not seem to need. The innkeeper, a heavy woman named Ilse, gave her the room above the kitchen and asked no questions, because in a village of two hundred and six souls, questions were the one thing everybody already had the answers to. The stranger paid in coins that were slightly too old, thanked her in an accent nobody could place, and went to bed without eating.

At dawn she was gone. In her room, on the small table under the window, lay the map, unfolded now, and on it a single route traced in pencil from the harbour up the cliff path to the lighthouse door. Beside the map stood a brass key, green with age, and a note written in careful, looping handwriting: "Some lights are only waiting to be asked." Ilse read it twice, put the key in her apron pocket, and walked up the cliff path as the gulls wheeled over the water. The door, which had been locked since before her own daughter was born, opened without a sound. Inside, the air smelled of oil and salt and something older, like rain on warm stone. She climbed the one hundred and forty steps slowly, counting each one aloud, and when she reached the top she found the great lamp polished and ready, a box of matches resting on the lens as though someone had only stepped away for a moment. She struck one. The flame was small, but the glass took it and made it enormous, and out across the grey water a long golden beam swung round to find the boats.

note: long English technical passage
text:
Autoregressive language models generate text one token at a time, and each new token requires attention over every previous token in the context. To avoid recomputing the key and value projections for the whole prefix at each step, inference engines keep them in a key-value cache. The cache grows linearly with the sequence length: for a model with L layers, H key-value heads, and head dimension D, storing keys and values in 16-bit precision costs 2 x 2 x L x H x D bytes per token. For long contexts this memory traffic, not the arithmetic, dominates the decode step, which is why so much engineering effort goes into compressing the cache.

Several families of techniques attack the problem. Grouped-query attention shares each key-value head among several query heads. Multi-head latent attention projects the keys and values into a low-rank latent vector and reconstructs them on demand, so only the latent needs to be stored. Linear-attention and state-space layers replace the growing cache with a fixed-size recurrent state that is updated once per token: the state has the same footprint at ten tokens as at ten million, though it must summarize the past lossily. Hybrid architectures interleave a few full-attention layers, which retain exact recall, with many recurrent layers, which are cheap.

Quantization is the other main lever. Weights stored in four-bit groups with a per-group scale and zero point shrink the model by roughly a factor of four relative to 16-bit weights, and the decode kernels dequantize on the fly in registers so that memory bandwidth is the only cost. The quality loss is measured by comparing the next-token distributions of the quantized and reference models over a held-out text, typically using the Kullback-Leibler divergence averaged over positions; a mean divergence below 0.01 nats is usually considered visually indistinguishable in generation. Speculative decoding adds yet another multiplier: a small draft model proposes several tokens, the large model verifies them in a single batched pass, and any accepted prefix is kept, so the expected number of tokens per large-model pass exceeds one without changing the output distribution.

text:
"Did you remember the tickets?" Maya asked, balancing a paper cup of coffee on top of her suitcase.

"Of course I did," said Dev. He patted his jacket, then his trousers, then the jacket again. "They're right here. Well. They were right here."

"Dev."

"I'm kidding! Look, here they are. Gate 14, departure at 7:45. We have plenty of time."

"We have forty minutes, and you want to stop for pastries." She narrowed her eyes. "I know that look."

"It's not a look. It's a plan. Nobody ever regretted a croissant at an airport."

"I regretted the one in Lisbon."

"That was a pastel de nata, and you ate four of them, so that is on you." Dev grinned and started walking toward the bakery counter anyway. Maya sighed, dragged her suitcase after him, and caught up just as he was ordering in his terrible, cheerful French. The woman behind the counter answered in perfect English, which only encouraged him.

"Two croissants, one with almond, and... what do you want, Maya?"

"Nothing. We are going to miss the flight."

"We are not going to miss the flight. Almond for her too, please." He handed over a crumpled ten-euro note. "See? Efficient. Delicious. Under budget."

She took the bag from him, peeked inside, and the corner of her mouth betrayed her. "Fine. But if they close the gate, you are explaining it to my mother."

"Deal," he said. "She likes me better than she likes you anyway."

"That," said Maya, already hurrying toward security, "is the most dangerous thing you've said all week."

They joined the queue behind a family of five and a man arguing quietly with his phone. Dev ate his croissant in three bites, brushed the flakes from his scarf, and offered the other half of Maya's almond one to a small boy, who accepted it with great seriousness. "Sixteen minutes," Maya whispered. "Fifteen and a half," said Dev, "but who is counting?"
